section.title: Duties and Portions of the Priests
section.sectionRationale: Closing the long unit that began with Korah's rebellion and Aaron's budded staff, this chapter settles the practical question those crises raised, who bears the risk and the responsibility of the sanctuary, and answers it with generous provision: the priests and Levites will have no land inheritance among the tribes because the LORD Himself, and the tithes given to Him, will be their portion.
section.thesis: Aaron and his sons bear the weighty responsibility for any offense involving the sanctuary, while the Levites assist them, and in exchange for this life devoted entirely to God's service, both priests and Levites receive their portion not in land but directly from God's own provision, the sacred offerings and the tithe, showing that those set apart to serve God most closely find their true inheritance in Him rather than in property.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Aaron and his sons bearing the responsibility for the sanctuary and priesthood, with the Levites given to assist and protect them; the priests' portions from the holy and sacred offerings of Israel; the LORD Himself declared to be Aaron's portion and inheritance, with the Levites given the tithe instead of land; and the Levites required to give a tithe of their tithe to the priests.

units.label: Aaron and the Levites bear the responsibility

verses.text: So the LORD said to Aaron, “You and your sons and your father's house must bear the iniquity involving the sanctuary. And you and your sons alone must bear the iniquity involving your priesthood.
But bring with you also your brothers from the tribe of Levi, the tribe of your father, that they may join you and assist you and your sons before the Tent of the Testimony.
And they shall attend to your duties and to all the duties of the Tent; but they must not come near to the furnishings of the sanctuary or the altar, or both they and you will die.
They are to join you and attend to the duties of the Tent of Meeting, doing all the work at the Tent; but no outsider may come near you.
And you shall attend to the duties of the sanctuary and of the altar, so that wrath may not fall on the Israelites again.
Behold, I Myself have selected your fellow Levites from the Israelites as a gift to you, dedicated to the LORD to perform the service for the Tent of Meeting.

But only you and your sons shall attend to your priesthood for everything concerning the altar and what is inside the veil, and you are to perform that service. I am giving you the work of the priesthood as a gift, but any outsider who comes near the sanctuary must be put to death.”

units.label: The priests' portions from the offerings

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Aaron, “Behold, I have put you in charge of My offerings. As for all the sacred offerings of the Israelites, I have given them to you and your sons as a portion and a permanent statute.

A portion of the most holy offerings reserved from the fire will be yours. From all the offerings they render to Me as most holy offerings, whether grain offerings or sin offerings or guilt offerings, that part belongs to you and your sons.
You are to eat it as a most holy offering, and every male may eat it. You shall regard it as holy.

And this is yours as well: the offering of their gifts, along with all the wave offerings of the Israelites. I have given this to you and your sons and daughters as a permanent statute. Every ceremonially clean person in your household may eat it.
I give you all the freshest olive oil and all the finest new wine and grain that the Israelites give to the LORD as their firstfruits.
The firstfruits of everything in their land that they bring to the LORD will belong to you. Every ceremonially clean person in your household may eat them.
Every devoted thing in Israel belongs to you.
The firstborn of every womb, whether man or beast, that is offered to the LORD belongs to you. But you must surely redeem every firstborn son and every firstborn male of unclean animals.
You are to pay the redemption price for a month-old male according to your valuation: five shekels of silver, according to the sanctuary shekel, which is twenty gerahs.

But you must not redeem the firstborn of an ox, a sheep, or a goat; they are holy. You are to sprinkle their blood on the altar and burn their fat as an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
And their meat belongs to you, just as the breast and right thigh of the wave offering belong to you.

All the holy offerings that the Israelites present to the LORD I give to you and to your sons and daughters as a permanent statute. It is a permanent covenant of salt before the LORD for you and your offspring.”

units.label: The LORD is Aaron's inheritance
units.note: the Levites given the tithe instead of land

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Aaron, “You will have no {{inheritance|inheritance}} in their land, nor will you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites.
Behold, I have given to the Levites all the tithes in Israel as an inheritance in return for the work they do, the service of the Tent of Meeting.
No longer may the Israelites come near to the Tent of Meeting, or they will incur guilt and die.

The Levites are to perform the work of the Tent of Meeting, and they must bear their iniquity. This is a permanent statute for the generations to come. The Levites will not receive an inheritance among the Israelites.

For I have given to the Levites as their inheritance the tithe that the Israelites present to the LORD as a contribution. That is why I told them that they would not receive an inheritance among the Israelites.”

units.label: The Levites' tithe of the tithe

verses.text: And the LORD instructed Moses,

“Speak to the Levites and tell them: ‘When you receive from the Israelites the tithe that I have given you as your inheritance, you must present part of it as an offering to the LORD, a tithe of the tithe.
Your offering will be reckoned to you as grain from the threshing floor or juice from the winepress.
So you are to present an offering to the LORD from all the tithes you receive from the Israelites, and from these you are to give the LORD's offering to Aaron the priest.
You must present the offering due the LORD from all the best of every gift, the holiest part of it.’
Therefore say to the Levites, ‘When you have presented the best part, it will be reckoned to you as the produce of the threshing floor or winepress.
And you and your households may eat the rest of it anywhere; it is the compensation for your work at the Tent of Meeting.
Once you have presented the best part of it, you will not incur guilt because of it. But you must not defile the sacred offerings of the Israelites, or else you will die.’”

inheritance.gloss: Inheritance or portion, the same word normally used for tribal land allotments in Canaan. Declaring that the LORD Himself is Aaron's nachalah deliberately substitutes God for territory, reframing what could look like exclusion from land as instead the greatest possible inheritance.

basic.context: As the long section of rebellion narratives closes, God settles the practical arrangements for priestly and Levitical support: Aaron and his sons bear full responsibility for any offense involving the sanctuary, the Levites assist and protect them from unauthorized approach, and in place of a land inheritance among the tribes, the priests receive a portion of Israel's sacred offerings while the Levites receive the tithe, out of which they in turn give a tenth to the priests.
basic.hermeneutics: This is practical, historical legislation establishing the material support system for Israel's priesthood and Levites. Its key theological claim, that the LORD Himself is Aaron's portion and inheritance rather than land, verse 20, reframes what might look like a merely administrative arrangement as a statement about where true security and identity are ultimately found.
basic.originalLanguages: The declaration that the LORD is Aaron's nachalah, portion and inheritance, uses the very term normally used for tribal land allotments in Canaan, deliberately substituting God Himself for territory, so that Aaron's priestly line possesses something greater than any plot of ground, the LORD's own presence and provision as their lasting share.
basic.typology: The priesthood receiving no land inheritance, but the LORD Himself as their portion, anticipates believers whose true inheritance is not an earthly possession but God Himself, kept for them in heaven, and ultimately anticipates Christ, our great High Priest, whose reward is not territorial but relational, seated at the Father's right hand.
basic.christ: Where Aaron and his sons bore the weighty risk of guilt involving the sanctuary and depended entirely on God's provision rather than land, Christ, our true and greater High Priest, bore the full weight of guilt for sin once for all, Hebrews 9:26, and now, having no need of any earthly inheritance, has been given the name above every name and reigns as our eternal mediator.
basic.god: God provides generously for those He calls to serve Him closely, ensuring the priests and Levites are cared for through the very offerings brought to Him rather than left to fend for themselves. He also holds them to serious responsibility, since bearing the guilt of the sanctuary is no light matter, showing that closeness to God's service carries both privilege and weight.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 10:9 and 18:1-2 echo this chapter's declaration that the LORD, not land, is the Levites' inheritance. Hebrews 9:26 describes Christ's once-for-all bearing of sin, surpassing the priests' ongoing responsibility here. 1 Peter 1:4 describes believers' inheritance kept in heaven, incorruptible and unfading.
basic.oneStory: God provides generously for those set apart to serve Him, giving them Himself as their true portion rather than land, and requiring careful responsibility in exchange for the privilege of nearness to His holy things. That pattern of costly service and God-given inheritance culminates in Christ, our great High Priest, who bore the full weight of sin and now shares His inheritance with all who are united to Him by faith.

context.literary:
Numbers 18 is God's answer to the question that closed chapter 17: 'Anyone who comes near the tabernacle of the LORD will die. Are we all going to perish?' Numbers 17:13. The chapter answers in two ways. First it sets a guard, so that no one wanders into death. Then it sets up the gifts that will keep that guard in place for generations.

The chapter is built from four speeches. Three begin 'the LORD said to Aaron,' verses 1, 8 and 20, which is unusual, since the LORD normally speaks to Moses, and Aaron is addressed directly only rarely, as in Leviticus 10:8. The fourth speech, verses 25 to 32, goes through Moses to the Levites. The effect is that Aaron hears his own charge, his own provision and his own inheritance from God's mouth, just after God has confirmed him with the budding staff.

The speeches move from duty to provision to identity and back to duty. Verses 1 to 7 say who guards what. Verses 8 to 19 list what the priests receive. Verses 20 to 24 declare that God is Aaron's portion and give the tithe to the Levites. Verses 25 to 32 require the Levites to give a tenth of what they receive.

Two frames hold it together. The chapter opens with Aaron's house bearing 'the iniquity involving the sanctuary,' verse 1, and it ends with the Levites told that once they give the best part 'you will not incur guilt,' verse 32, which in Hebrew is the same idiom of bearing sin. Warnings of death also sound through the text at verses 3, 7, 22 and 32. The chapter never forgets that holiness kills the careless. Yet threaded between those warnings is the language of gift: the Levites are 'a gift,' verse 6, the priesthood is 'a gift,' verse 7, and the offerings are 'given,' verses 8, 11, 12, 19, 21 and 24. Guarded holiness and lavish giving sit side by side.
context.historical:
The priests and Levites were a tribe without territory. When the land was divided under Joshua, 'to the tribe of Levi, however, Moses had given no inheritance,' Joshua 13:14. They received cities with pasturelands scattered among the other tribes, Numbers 35:2, and lived from what the people brought to the sanctuary. Their welfare depended directly on Israel's faithfulness.

The offerings listed in verses 8 to 19 fall into two grades. The most holy portions, the priests' share of grain offerings, sin offerings and guilt offerings, were eaten only by the males of the priestly family, and Leviticus specifies 'in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting,' Leviticus 6:26. The BSB footnote to verse 10 notes that the phrase can be read 'in a most holy place.' The lesser holy portions, the wave offerings, firstfruits and firstborn, could be eaten by the whole priestly household, sons and daughters alike, provided they were ceremonially clean, verses 11 and 13.

The firstborn rule rests on the Passover. God had claimed every firstborn of Israel when He struck the firstborn of Egypt, Numbers 3:12-13. Clean animals were sacrificed. Firstborn sons and unclean animals were redeemed, sons at five shekels of silver, verse 16, the same price set when the Levites were counted in place of the firstborn, Numbers 3:47. The BSB footnote gives the weight as about 57 grams of silver.

Israel's history shows how fragile the system was. Hezekiah had to command the people 'to make a contribution for the priests and Levites so that they could devote themselves to the Law of the LORD,' 2 Chronicles 31:4. After the exile Nehemiah found that 'the portions for the Levites had not been given to them' and the Levites had 'gone back to their own fields,' Nehemiah 13:10. Malachi called withholding the tithe robbing God, Malachi 3:8. Neglect of the tithe was not a small budget matter; it emptied the sanctuary of those who served it.
context.canonical:
This chapter is the foundation for everything Scripture later says about Levi's inheritance. Deuteronomy repeats it twice: 'the LORD is his inheritance,' Deuteronomy 10:9, and 'they are to eat the offerings made by fire to the LORD; that is their inheritance,' Deuteronomy 18:1-2. Joshua sets it down at the division of the land, once in terms of the offerings, Joshua 13:14, and once in terms of God Himself, Joshua 13:33. Ezekiel's vision of the restored temple restates it: 'I am their inheritance... for I am their possession,' Ezekiel 44:28.

The Psalms and prophets turn the priestly privilege into a personal confession. 'The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup,' Psalm 16:5. 'God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever,' Psalm 73:26. 'You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living,' Psalm 142:5. In the ruins of Jerusalem, 'The LORD is my portion,' says my soul, 'therefore I will hope in Him,' Lamentations 3:24. What began as the inheritance of one tribe becomes the hope of any believer who has lost everything else.

The tithe system is traced forward to Nehemiah's covenant, Nehemiah 10:37-38, which follows Numbers 18 closely, including the tenth of the tithes brought to the storerooms. Malachi's challenge to 'bring the full tithe into the storehouse,' Malachi 3:10, assumes this chapter.

In the New Testament, Paul appeals to this chapter's logic when he writes that 'those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings' and so 'those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel,' 1 Corinthians 9:13-14. Hebrews notes that 'the law commands the sons of Levi who become priests to collect a tenth,' Hebrews 7:5, and then argues that Levi paid a tenth through Abraham to Melchizedek, Hebrews 7:9-10. Peter gives the priestly inheritance to all believers, 'an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading,' 1 Peter 1:4, and calls the church 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses records these laws to answer a frightened people and a newly confirmed priesthood at the same time. To the people, the message is that God has not left them exposed to His holiness. The priests and Levites will stand between them and the sanctuary 'so that wrath may not fall on the Israelites again,' verse 5. The terror of Numbers 17:12-13 is met with an arrangement, not a rebuke.

To Aaron and his sons, the message is double. Their office is a gift, verse 7, and it is a weight. They bear the iniquity involving the sanctuary, verse 1. If an outsider encroaches, or if they themselves are careless, the consequences fall on them. Nearness to God is an honor that cannot be treated lightly.

To the Levites, the message is that they are provided for and still accountable. The tithes are theirs as wages 'in return for the work they do,' verse 21, and yet they too must give, and give the best. No one in Israel stood outside the circle of giving to God, not even those who lived by the giving of others.

Behind all of this lies the claim of verse 20, 'I am your portion and your inheritance.' Moses wants Aaron's house, and every reader after them, to see that having God is worth more than having land. Every other tribe would measure its security in fields. Aaron's house was to measure it in the LORD.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter prescribes a system for Israel's sanctuary, and in its original form it applies to a temple and priesthood that no longer stand. The New Testament does not command the church to maintain a Levitical order, to redeem firstborn sons for five shekels, or to bring firstfruits to a priest. Christ's once for all sacrifice has ended the sacrificial portions, Hebrews 9:26.

Several principles do carry forward, and the New Testament names them. Those who give themselves to the ministry of the word should be supported by those they serve, 1 Corinthians 9:13-14 and Galatians 6:6. Giving should be proportionate and regular, 1 Corinthians 16:2, and cheerful rather than compelled, 2 Corinthians 9:7. Those who receive support are themselves called to give, as the Levites gave a tithe of their tithe. And God's people offer the best, not the leftovers, verse 29.

Most deeply, the declaration that God is His servants' portion is not limited to the priests of Israel. The Psalms already apply it to any faithful worshipper, and the New Testament extends the priestly inheritance to all believers, Colossians 1:12.

debates.question: Why does the LORD, rather than land, become Aaron's inheritance?

views.label: A theological statement about the worth of nearness to God
views.case: Every other tribe received territory, and the text makes a point of denying it to Aaron: 'You will have no inheritance in their land,' verse 20. The contrast is intended. God Himself is presented as a greater share than any field, and the Psalms take the priestly phrase as a confession of faith, Psalm 16:5 and 73:26.

views.label: A practical arrangement for a priesthood serving the whole nation
views.case: The Levites were to live in cities scattered through every tribe, Numbers 35:2, teaching and serving all Israel. A single territory would have tied them to one region. Their support from the tithes of all the tribes fitted their national role.

debates.bearing: The two views are not rivals. The practical arrangement was the means; the theological statement is the meaning. God's provision for His servants came through His people's gifts, but what He gave them was Himself, and that is why the words could be taken up by anyone who trusts Him.

debates.question: Whose iniquity do the Levites bear in verse 23?

views.label: The iniquity of the Israelites
views.case: The sentence follows immediately on verse 22, 'No longer may the Israelites come near... or they will incur guilt and die.' Read this way, the Levites absorb the liability for any Israelite who encroaches on the sanctuary. They stand as a buffer, so that the penalty that would break out against the whole people falls instead on the guards.

views.label: Their own iniquity
views.case: The pronoun can equally refer to the Levites themselves: if they fail in their duty, they will answer for it. This matches verse 3, where both Levites and priests will die if the Levites touch the sacred furnishings, and verse 32, which warns them against defiling the offerings.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew allows both, and the chapter supports both. The Levites were accountable for their own failures, and their faithfulness shielded the congregation. Either way the principle is clear: those who serve near God stand in a costly place on behalf of others.

debates.question: Is the tithe binding on Christians?

views.label: The tithe remains a standard
views.case: Tithing appears before the law, when Abram gave Melchizedek 'a tenth of everything,' Genesis 14:20, and Jacob vowed a tenth, Genesis 28:22. Jesus did not dismiss the Pharisees' tithing, saying they should have practiced justice and mercy 'without neglecting the former,' Matthew 23:23. On this view a tenth is a fitting baseline for Christian giving.

views.label: The tithe belonged to the Levitical system
views.case: Numbers 18 ties the tithe to the Levites and the tabernacle, which Christ has fulfilled. The New Testament letters never command a tenth. They speak instead of giving in proportion, 1 Corinthians 16:2, and willingly, 2 Corinthians 9:7. On this view generosity is required, but a fixed percentage is not.

debates.bearing: Both sides agree that God's people are to support those who teach the word and to give generously, first to God and from the best. The pattern of Numbers 18, where even the receivers give, argues against treating any percentage as a ceiling. Freedom in Christ is freedom to give more gladly, not less.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter opens with the phrase 'bear the iniquity,' nasa avon, verse 1. The verb nasa means to lift or carry, and avon is iniquity or the guilt it brings. The phrase can describe someone who bears the consequences of his own sin, but it can also describe one who carries guilt on behalf of others. It is used of the gold plate on Aaron's forehead, by which he would 'bear the iniquity of the holy things,' Exodus 28:38, and of the goat of the Day of Atonement, which 'will carry on itself all their iniquities,' Leviticus 16:22. Isaiah uses the same vocabulary of the Servant: 'He will bear their iniquities,' Isaiah 53:11. Numbers 18 places the priests and Levites in this role of carrying the liability of the sanctuary so that it does not fall on the people.

The Levites are 'a gift,' verse 6, and the priesthood itself is 'the work of the priesthood as a gift,' verse 7, literally a 'service of gift.' The noun mattanah is used for a present freely given. Numbers 8:19 had already said 'I have given the Levites as a gift to Aaron.' The Levites are given to Aaron; the priesthood is given to Aaron; the offerings are given to Aaron. The verb give, natan, runs through the chapter like a refrain.

The word translated 'offerings' and 'contribution' in verses 8, 11, 24 and 26 is terumah. It comes from the root rum, to be high or lifted, and describes a portion lifted off from a larger whole and set apart for God. Older translations called it a 'heave offering.' The tithe is the Israelites' terumah to the LORD, verse 24, and the tithe of the tithe is the Levites' terumah, verse 26. What God receives, He hands on to His servants.

In verse 14, 'every devoted thing' translates cherem, a word for anything irrevocably handed over to God. Leviticus 27:28 says that nothing so devoted can be sold or redeemed, for 'everything so devoted is most holy to the LORD.' The same word describes Jericho, 'devoted to the LORD for destruction,' Joshua 6:17. Whether destroyed or given to the sanctuary, what is cherem can never return to common use.

Verse 19 calls the arrangement 'a permanent covenant of salt,' which the BSB footnote explains as 'a perpetual covenant.' Salt preserves and does not decay. Every grain offering was seasoned with 'the salt of the covenant of your God,' Leviticus 2:13, and Abijah later calls God's gift of kingship to David 'a covenant of salt,' 2 Chronicles 13:5. The phrase marks a bond meant to last.

Twice the Levites are told that their offering 'will be reckoned to you,' verses 27 and 30. The verb is chashav, to count or credit, the verb of Genesis 15:6, 'it was credited to him as righteousness.' The Levites own no fields or vineyards, yet God counts their gift as if it were grain from their own threshing floor.

Finally, the word for 'the best' in verses 12, 29, 30 and 32 is chelev, literally fat. The fat of every sacrifice belonged to God, 'All the fat is the LORD's,' Leviticus 3:16. To give 'the best part' is to give God the portion that was always His.

typology.type: The priests who bear the iniquity of the sanctuary, Numbers 18:1
typology.fulfillment: Aaron's house carried the liability for anything that went wrong at God's dwelling so that wrath would not fall on the people, verse 5. Christ carries far more. He 'was offered once to bear the sins of many,' Hebrews 9:28, and 'Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24, fulfilling Isaiah's Servant who 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12. The type falls short in that Aaron's house bore a risk and a responsibility, and could itself fall under wrath. Christ bore the actual guilt and its penalty, and did so once for all, Hebrews 9:26.

typology.type: The LORD as the priests' portion instead of land, Numbers 18:20
typology.fulfillment: Aaron had no field, only God. In Christ, every believer is given that priestly inheritance. God has 'qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light,' Colossians 1:12, and believers are 'heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ,' Romans 8:17. The Spirit is 'the pledge of our inheritance,' Ephesians 1:14. The escalation is that the inheritance is no longer limited to one tribe, and it includes, rather than replaces, a renewed creation, since the Son is 'heir of all things,' Hebrews 1:2.

typology.type: The Levites given to Aaron as a gift, Numbers 18:6
typology.fulfillment: The Levites were taken from Israel and given to the high priest to serve with him. Jesus speaks of His disciples in the same terms: 'They were Yours; You gave them to Me,' John 17:6, and Hebrews puts on His lips, 'Here am I, and the children God has given Me,' Hebrews 2:13. The risen Christ in turn gives gifts to His church, 'some to be apostles, some to be prophets,' Ephesians 4:11. The correspondence is real, but where the Levites were kept at a distance from the altar, Christ's people are brought into the Most Holy Place with Him.

typology.type: The redemption of the firstborn for five shekels, Numbers 18:15-16
typology.fulfillment: Every firstborn son belonged to God and had to be bought back. Luke records that Jesus' parents brought Him to the temple because 'Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord,' Luke 2:23. The One presented as a firstborn needing redemption is Himself 'the firstborn from the dead,' Revelation 1:5, whose people were redeemed 'not with perishable things such as silver or gold' but 'with the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18-19. The type is inverted in Christ: the firstborn does not merely get redeemed, He becomes the redemption.

study.christ:
Numbers 18 leads to Christ through the language of bearing. The chapter's first sentence gives Aaron's house the weight of 'the iniquity involving the sanctuary.' They were to stand between a holy God and a fragile people, carrying the risk of encroachment on themselves so that wrath would not fall on the congregation, verse 5. Isaiah later describes a Servant who takes this role to its limit: 'He will bear their iniquities... He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors,' Isaiah 53:11-12. The New Testament says this is Jesus, who 'was offered once to bear the sins of many,' Hebrews 9:28. Aaron's house guarded the sanctuary against sin. Christ bore sin in Himself and took it away.

It leads to Christ through the language of inheritance. Aaron was told that the LORD was his portion, not the land. Jesus lived that out in a way no priest had. He had 'no place to lay His head,' Matthew 8:20. He owned no land, and He lived wholly from the Father's provision. Yet He is the one whom God 'appointed heir of all things,' Hebrews 1:2. The priest who had nothing is the heir of everything, and He shares that inheritance: believers are 'co-heirs with Christ,' Romans 8:17.

It leads to Christ through the language of gift. Aaron received the Levites as a gift. Jesus speaks of those the Father has given Him, John 17:6. Aaron received the priesthood as a gift. Christ also 'did not take upon Himself the glory of becoming a high priest,' Hebrews 5:5; it was given by the Father.

It leads to Christ by contrast. The priests were supported by a constant stream of sacrifices; every sin offering fed them because sin kept needing offerings. Christ's priesthood does not live on continual sacrifice. 'He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself,' Hebrews 9:26.

And the chapter's quiet ending points forward to a greater priest. The Levites give a tenth of their tithes to Aaron, and Hebrews argues that Levi himself, in Abraham, paid a tenth to Melchizedek, Hebrews 7:9-10. Even the tithe chain of Numbers 18 bows to a priest outside Levi, and 'the lesser is blessed by the greater,' Hebrews 7:7. That priest is Christ, a priest forever. The details of portions and shekels are not hidden pictures of Jesus, but the shape of the chapter, a priest bearing guilt, living from God alone and receiving the tithe of the tithe, is a shape He fills.
study.god:
This chapter shows God as the Holy One who makes a way to live near Him. He does not lower the danger. Warnings of death recur at verses 3, 7, 22 and 32. Instead He builds a structure within which His people can be safe: priests at the altar, Levites around the tent, and a permanent statute so that wrath need not fall again, verse 5. God's holiness and His desire to dwell among His people are held together by the provision He makes.

He is lavish. The chapter is full of giving. He gives the Levites to Aaron, gives the priesthood as a gift, gives the offerings, gives the tithe, and finally gives Himself. The offerings the people bring are not kept by God for Himself; He passes them on to feed His servants and their sons and daughters. The God who receives is the God who shares.

He is faithful. The arrangement is 'a permanent statute,' verses 8, 11, 19 and 23, and 'a permanent covenant of salt,' verse 19. What God gives He does not take back on a whim. Even after Korah's rebellion by a Levite, God does not withdraw His provision from Levi.

He cares for His servants' material needs. It would be possible to spiritualize the chapter entirely, but the text is concrete: oil, wine, grain, firstborn animals, silver. God knows His priests must eat. He does not tell them to live on air because they have Him as their portion; He gives Himself as their portion and feeds them through His people.

He expects the best. The Levites give 'from all the best of every gift, the holiest part of it,' verse 29. God is not honored by leftovers. The word used is the word for the fat, the part that always belonged to Him.

He is Himself the highest good. 'I am your portion and your inheritance,' verse 20. The claim assumes that God is more to be desired than land, harvests or security. The Psalms take this up, 'my portion forever,' Psalm 73:26. For worship, the chapter teaches us to value God above what He gives, to support those who serve His word, to give Him the best, and to trust that the One who asks is the One who provides.

crossReferences.note: The people's terrified cry, 'Anyone who comes near the tabernacle of the LORD will die,' is the question Numbers 18 answers. The guard of priests and Levites is God's reply, set up so that wrath will not fall on the Israelites again, Numbers 18:5. The chapter should be read as the sequel to that cry.

God took the Levites in place of every firstborn Israelite, claiming the firstborn since the night He struck Egypt. This explains verse 15 of Numbers 18, where firstborn animals are given to the priests and firstborn sons must be redeemed. The Passover stands behind the firstborn law.

The gold plate on Aaron's forehead enables him to 'bear the iniquity of the holy things.' Numbers 18:1 applies the same responsibility to Aaron's whole house. Both texts show the priest carrying on himself what would otherwise endanger the worshippers.

Moses restates this chapter for the generation entering the land: the Levitical priests 'shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel,' they eat the offerings, and 'the LORD is their inheritance.' Deuteronomy confirms that Numbers 18 was meant to govern life in Canaan.

David takes the priestly words of Numbers 18:20 as his own: 'The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup.' He even uses the language of boundary lines, the vocabulary of land allotment. The inheritance of Levi becomes the confession of a king and of every believer.

In the ruins of Jerusalem, with land and temple lost, the poet says, 'The LORD is my portion... therefore I will hope in Him.' When every tribe had lost its land, the priestly inheritance of Numbers 18:20 was the only one left standing.

Nehemiah discovers the Levites had gone back to their fields because their portions had not been given. The failure shows how directly the sanctuary depended on the people's obedience to Numbers 18, and how quickly neglect emptied God's house of its servants.

God charges Israel with robbing Him 'in tithes and offerings' and commands, 'Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in My house.' The storehouse and the food are the Levites' portion of Numbers 18:21-24.

Paul argues from this chapter that 'those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings,' and so 'the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel.' The principle of Numbers 18 is carried into the church without its sacrificial system.

Hebrews notes that the law commands the Levites 'to collect a tenth,' as Numbers 18:21 establishes, and then argues that Levi paid a tenth through Abraham to Melchizedek. The chain of tithes in this chapter is used to show a greater priesthood than Aaron's.

Aaron's house bore the iniquity of the sanctuary continually, with offerings brought every day. Christ 'has appeared once for all... to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself' and 'was offered once to bear the sins of many,' completing the bearing that the priests could only manage.

Peter describes 'an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you.' The priests had God instead of land; believers have an inheritance secured by the resurrection that no loss can take away, the priestly portion extended to the whole church.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God gave humanity a garden and Himself. After the fall the gift of land and the gift of His presence were pulled apart; Adam was sent out to work cursed ground, far from the tree of life. God's promise to Abraham reunited them: a land, and 'I will be their God,' Genesis 17:8. Numbers 18 shows one tribe given the second gift without the first. Levi receives no field at all, only the LORD.

That arrangement sets up a pattern the rest of Scripture uses. Israel's other tribes inherited land, and in time they lost it. The exile left Jerusalem desolate, and the poet of Lamentations had only one inheritance left: 'The LORD is my portion,' Lamentations 3:24. The priestly inheritance proved to be the one that survived when every other was gone. The prophets looked forward to a day when all God's people would be called 'the priests of the LORD,' Isaiah 61:6.

The chapter also sets up the problem of priestly bearing. Aaron's house guarded the sanctuary by carrying its liability, day after day, and the sacrifices never ended. Israel needed a priest who could bear guilt once and finally.

Redemption arrives in Christ. He bears the sins of many, Hebrews 9:28. He lives without land and yet is heir of all things, Hebrews 1:2. He makes His people 'a kingdom, priests to His God and Father,' Revelation 1:6. Every believer now shares Levi's portion: God Himself, with an inheritance that is imperishable, 1 Peter 1:4.

The story ends where the two gifts are finally rejoined. In the new creation there is land again, a whole renewed earth, and the voice from the throne says, 'the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them,' Revelation 21:3. There is no temple in the city, 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. There is no longer any need for guards at the tent or tithes for a sanctuary. The whole people of God has what Aaron was promised: the LORD as their portion forever, in a land that will never be lost.

quiz.q: What responsibility did Aaron and his sons bear according to the opening of this chapter?

options.text: The iniquity involving the sanctuary and their priesthood, so that no outsider could approach without guilt.
options.note: Verses 1 and 7 state this responsibility exactly.

options.text: The responsibility of leading Israel's army in battle.
options.note: This is not the responsibility described in this chapter.

options.text: The responsibility of collecting the census figures each year.
options.note: This is not described anywhere in this chapter.

options.note: Verses 1 and 7 describe this responsibility directly.

quiz.q: What role did the Levites play according to this chapter?

options.text: To join Aaron and his sons, assisting with the duties of the Tent of Meeting, though not permitted to approach the furnishings of the sanctuary or the altar themselves.
options.note: Verses 2 to 4 describe this exact role and its limits.

options.text: To serve as the only ones permitted to enter the Most Holy Place.
options.note: This contradicts the text; that access belonged only to the high priest, not the Levites generally.

options.text: To replace the priesthood entirely going forward.
options.note: This contradicts the ongoing distinction between priests and Levites maintained throughout the chapter.

options.text: No role for the Levites is described.
options.note: Verses 2 to 4 describe their role in detail.

quiz.q: What did the priests receive instead of a land inheritance among the Israelites?

options.text: A portion of the sacred offerings, including the most holy offerings and the firstfruits.
options.note: Verses 8 to 19 describe this provision in detail.

options.text: A fixed annual salary paid directly from a royal treasury.
options.note: This is not the arrangement described in verses 8 to 19.

options.note: This is not stated anywhere in the text.

options.text: No alternative provision is described.

quiz.q: What were the Levites required to do with the tithes they received from the Israelites?

options.text: Present a tithe of the tithe as an offering to the LORD, giving this portion to Aaron the priest.
options.note: Verses 26 to 28 describe this requirement exactly.

options.note: This contradicts the explicit instruction to tithe from their tithe in verses 26 to 28.

options.note: This contradicts the specific instruction given to the Levites regarding Aaron's portion.

options.text: No further instruction about the tithe is given.
options.note: Verses 26 to 28 give further instruction directly.

questions: Aaron and his sons bore serious, weighty responsibility for the sanctuary, a privilege that came with real risk. Where has God given you a responsibility that carries more weight than you initially realized, and how are you stewarding it?

The Levites assisted the priests but were not permitted to do everything the priests did, each serving within defined boundaries. How do you handle boundaries on your own role, especially when you might want to do more than you have been given to do?

God declared Himself to be Aaron's portion and inheritance rather than any plot of land. What would it look like for you to genuinely believe that having God Himself is a greater inheritance than any material security you are tempted to chase instead?

The priests depended entirely on the rest of Israel's faithfulness in bringing tithes and offerings for their material support. Who in your life depends on your faithfulness in giving or generosity, and are you providing for them as you should?

Even the Levites, who received the tithe, were required to tithe from what they received, showing that generosity flows all the way through, not stopping once you have received something yourself. Where might God be calling you to keep passing on generosity rather than treating what you receive as a final stopping point?

translationNotes.note: Bear the iniquity involving the sanctuary indicates Aaron and his family assume legal and spiritual responsibility for any failure in properly handling holy things, a serious weight attached to their unique access.
A permanent covenant of salt uses an ancient idiom for an unbreakable, enduring agreement, salt being a stable, incorruptible substance associated elsewhere with covenant meals and preservation.

All the tithes in Israel given to the Levites as their inheritance in place of land directly explains why later biblical books frequently mention the Levites alongside the poor, the widow, and the orphan as those requiring the community's active, ongoing generosity.
